sentences.text: FEVER's claims came from annotators who were shown a sentence sampled from Wikipedia introductory sections and asked to write claims about that sentence's entity.
The sentence pool came from the June 2017 Wikipedia dump: about 5,000 'most accessed pages' plus the pages hyperlinked from them were used.

Annotators were told to write claims containing a single piece of information, focusing on the entity its original Wikipedia page was about, and were permitted arbitrary complexity and varied expression for entities.

To avoid trivially verifiable claims, the authors supplied a dictionary of hyperlinked terms from the original sentence plus the first sentence of their Wikipedia pages, letting annotators add complexity in a controlled way.
Annotators also had to produce mutations of the original claims — altered versions that may or may not change whether Wikipedia supports them, or may even make them unverifiable.

Six mutation types were specified, modeled on Natural Logic Inference operators: paraphrasing, negation, substitution of an entity/relation with a similar or dissimilar one, and making the claim more general or more specific.

Because annotators struggled to produce non-trivial negations, the interface was redesigned to show all mutation types at once and to highlight mutations containing 'not', and an ontology diagram was provided to illustrate entity similarity and class membership.
This process yielded claims with a mean length of 9.4 tokens, comparable to the 8.3-token average hypothesis length in the SNLI work of Bowman et al. (2015).

Claim generation was validated only implicitly, through the later claim labeling stage; 1.01% of claims were skipped, 2.11% had typos, and 6.63% were excluded as too vague or ambiguous (e.g. 'Sons of Anarchy premiered.').

The authors' later manual analysis of pipeline errors found 4.05% (n = 41) of claims did not meet the dataset guidelines, including tautological or self-contradictory claims and claims corrupted by named-entity mis-parsing.

ALCE assumes a naturallanguage question and a retrieval corpus, and requires building end-to-end systems to retrieve relevant passages from the corpus, generate a response to the question, and cite corresponding supporting passages. We compile three datasets that cover different types of questions and corpora— ASQA (Stelmakh et al., 2022), QAMPARI (Rubin et al., 2022), and ELI5 (Fan et al., 2019)—as shown in Table 1. Different from previous benchmarks (Lee et al., 2019; Bohnet et al., 2022), ALCE evaluates long-text generation, focusing on automatically evaluating citation quality, and allows citing multiple passages for individual statements. We design automatic evaluation methods in three dimensions: fluency, correctness, and citation quality. Specifically, we use MAUVE (Pillutla et al., 2021) to measure fluency, propose tailored correctness metrics for each dataset, and adopt a natural language inference (NLI) model (Honovich et al., 2022) to measure citation quality. We showcase how the three dimensions together contribute to a robust evaluation, preventing systems from exploiting shortcuts.
